title: The Heidelberg Catechism, Lord's Day 1
subtitle: The full text of Lord's Day 1 of the Heidelberg Catechism (1563) — 'What is thy only comfort in life and death?' — with notes on its history and design.
intro:
In 1563 Frederick III, the Elector Palatine, commissioned a catechism for his territory — a region caught between Lutheran and Reformed factions, exhausted by doctrinal warfare. The work fell chiefly to Zacharias Ursinus, a twenty-eight-year-old professor at Heidelberg. What he produced is the warmest doctrinal document of the Reformation: 129 questions arranged in fifty-two Lord's Days, one for each Sunday of the year, structured around guilt, grace, and gratitude. It begins not with God's existence or Scripture's authority but with a pastoral question — what is your only comfort in life and death?

The answer is one long sentence, and it is written in the first person singular. Not 'the believer's comfort is.' My comfort. That I am not my own. The catechism was designed to be learned by children and recited by the dying, and you can feel both audiences in every line. Frederick himself answered for it before the imperial Diet in 1566, when his crown was at stake, and did not retract a word.

Reprinted below is Lord's Day 1 complete — Questions 1 and 2 — the doorway through which the remaining fifty-one weeks pass. The rest of the catechism simply unfolds the three things named in Question 2: how great my sin is, how I am delivered, and how I am to be thankful. Four and a half centuries later, churches on every continent still open here. There are worse places to learn what Christianity claims. There may be none better.
text:
Lord's Day 1.

Question 1. What is thy only comfort in life and death?

Answer. That I with body and soul, both in life and death, am not my own, but belong unto my faithful Saviour Jesus Christ; who, with his precious blood, hath fully satisfied for all my sins, and delivered me from all the power of the devil; and so preserves me that without the will of my heavenly Father, not a hair can fall from my head; yea, that all things must be subservient to my salvation, and therefore, by his Holy Spirit, he also assures me of eternal life, and makes me sincerely willing and ready, henceforth, to live unto him.

Question 2. How many things are necessary for thee to know, that thou, enjoying this comfort, mayest live and die happily?

Answer. Three; the first, how great my sins and miseries are; the second, how I may be delivered from all my sins and miseries; the third, how I shall express my gratitude to God for such deliverance.

annotations.note: The German is Trost — solid consolation, ground to stand on, not a pleasant feeling. And 'only' is doing real work: the catechism opens by clearing away every rival comfort before naming the one that holds in death.

The most countercultural sentence in the document, then and now. The modern creed is self-ownership; the catechism calls belonging to another the best news available. Comfort begins exactly where autonomy ends. It is quoting 1 Corinthians 6:19–20.

annotations.phrase: with body and soul, both in life and death
annotations.note: Four totalities in nine words. Nothing of the person and no season of existence falls outside Christ's claim. The dying learned this line so they could say it when nothing else would come.

annotations.phrase: hath fully satisfied for all my sins
annotations.note: 'Satisfied' is the language of debt paid in full — not partially, not pending my contribution. The whole Reformation doctrine of justification is folded into one past-tense verb.

annotations.phrase: not a hair can fall from my head
annotations.note: Christ's own words (Luke 21:18; Matthew 10:30) turned into a doctrine of providence. The catechism does not promise that nothing painful will happen — it promises that nothing will happen apart from the Father's will, which is a different and harder comfort.

annotations.phrase: all things must be subservient to my salvation
annotations.note: An echo of Romans 8:28 with the force of 'must.' Not 'God will try to make the best of it.' Everything — including the worst things — is conscripted into the service of my salvation. This was written for people burying children, and it shows.

annotations.phrase: makes me sincerely willing and ready, henceforth, to live unto him
annotations.note: Comfort produces obedience; it is never produced by it. The order matters, and the whole catechism keeps it: gratitude is the third section, after deliverance, never the price of it.

annotations.phrase: Three; the first, how great my sins and miseries are
annotations.note: Question 2 lays out the catechism's architecture — guilt, grace, gratitude — which structures all 129 questions. Knowledge of sin comes first not to crush but to make the deliverance legible. You cannot treasure a rescue you never needed.
